thread:
Lina: Quick sync after the RFC: we still need a crisp contract between the Observer, Policy Manager, and Router for automated rollbacks/fallbacks. Who owns final actuation?
Marco: My vote: Router should be the only actuating component. Observer emits signals, Policy Manager evaluates and returns an ordered action list with confidence. Router executes. Keeps actuation path singular.
Kunal: Router-only actuation makes sense for consistency, but what about Dedicated clusters without Policy Manager access? We need an offline fallback mode where Router can evaluate a local policy.
Mei: Right. Suggestion: two operational modes: "centralized" (Policy Manager + Router) and "edge" (Router + local policy cache). Policy Manager publishes signed policy blobs with schema_version, TTL, and signature.
Lina: Sounds good. We also discussed action granularity: not just fallback to previous model. We should support multi-step degrade: reduce concurrency -> switch to quantized variant -> route to warm secondary -> full fallback.
Marco: Agreed. Policy response example (simplified): ```json
{"policy_version":"v1","ttl_ms":60000,"actions":[{"priority":10,"type":"reduce_concurrency","value":0.5},{"priority":20,"type":"variant_switch","variant":"v2-quantized"}]}
```
Kunal: Operational tradeoff: signed blobs are great, but what if policy TTL expires and Router goes offline? Need grace: Router can keep last-known policy for `grace_window_ms`. If no observer signals and no policy, default to `no_actuation`.
Mei: Oscillation avoidance: policy blobs should include `min_active_ms` and `cooldown_ms`. Router must atomically apply actions with a single source-of-truth id so rollbacks are idempotent. Logs should include `applied_policy_id`.
Lina: Security note: policy blobs must be verifiable (signature) and we should rate-limit policy fetches to avoid amplification attacks. Also a per-tenant allowlist for automatic fallback.
Marco: Tests: unit tests for Policy Manager evaluation (edge cases), Router integration tests that simulate rapid signal bursts, and a long-running soak with `fake-observer` producing intermittent spikes. Add a chaos test that drops policy blobs mid-apply.
Kunal: Runbook idea: if Router applies >2 distinct `hard_fallback` actions for the same tenant within 15m, auto-open incident state (pager) and set canary to 0% for that tenant. Alert metric: `sum(increases(router_applied_actions_total{action="hard_fallback"}[15m])) by (tenant) >= 2`.
Mei: For telemetry: emit `policy_eval_latency_ms`, `policy_blob_version`, `observer_lag_ms`, `router_applied_action{tenant,action,policy_id}`. Add tracing: policy_id parent -> router apply span.
Lina: Implementation ownership: Marco -> Router actuation primitives + local policy cache; Kunal -> Policy Manager API + signed blob format; Mei -> Telemetry + runbook fragments. I'll prototype a minimal signed-blob publisher and a `router-sim` harness.
devops-bot: devops-bot: Canary job queued: publish policy blob v1 for tenant=acme, rollout=10% -> 2024-10-03T14:00:00Z
Marco: One more design nuance: circuit-breaker for third-party observers. If observer source is flaky (missing >30s or producing contradictory signals), policy manager should mark `observer_health=poor` and Router must prefer conservative actions.
Kunal: For long-term refactor: think about policy-as-code. Authoring DSL that compiles to signed blobs. That lets SREs review policies in Git, run CI checks, then publish. Also helps per-tenant overrides.
Mei: Agreed. Action items: Marco -> start router shim + idempotent apply; Kunal -> draft signed blob spec and endpoint; Lina -> router-sim harness + soak tests; Mei -> alert rules and telemetry dashboard. Ping this thread when prototypes land. :white_check_mark:
